newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria says has no intention to devalue naira.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria says has no intention to devalue naira.

text.p: The Nigerian authorities said on Tuesday there were no plans to further devalue the naira currency and denounced as "unpatriotic" speculation to that effect.

"We wish to state categorically and with all emphasis at our command that government has no intention to further devalue the naira," finance minister Anthony Ani and central bank governor Paul Ogwuma said in a joint statement.

"With the current external reserve position of over $6 billion compared with $1.5 billion in the same period of 1996, the government is in a better position to defend the naira at all cost," they added.

The naira was devalued by 5.88 percent last month to 85 to the dollar at the autonomous foreign exchange market (AFEM) but there is widespread speculation that the authorities would have to further devalue it because of rising demand for forex at the weekly AFEM auctions.
Demand at recent auctions has hovered at around $100 million weekly compared with around $60 million weekly last year.
The authorities attributed the speculation to the drop in prices of crude oil, Nigeria's main foreign exchange earner.
The statement said banks and individuals who had been driving up demand for forex at the weekly auction had been identified through an audit of purchases on the market.
In January, the government removed restrictions on foreign exchange purchases for personal travel abroad which previously was fixed at $500.

"Unfortunately, some Nigerians took undue advantage of this gesture, in some cases people purchased $500,000 for personal travelling allowance and $1.8 million for basic travelling allowance," it said.
It said the persons and banks involved had been given till May 20 to return the excess together with accrued interest.
Nigeria operates an official exchange rate of 22 naira side by side with the AFEM but the official rate is reserved for only a few government transactions.
